content: Endometriosis is a condition that is often associated with chronic pain and infertility. Surgical interventions, particularly laparoscopic surgery, are designed to excise or ablate visible endometriotic lesions and restore normal pelvic anatomy. The purpose of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of laparoscopic surgery in managing pain and infertility caused by endometriosis. The review included 14 randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving 1,563 women diagnosed with endometriosis. These studies compared laparoscopic surgery to various other interventions, including diagnostic laparoscopy alone, laparoscopic ablation versus excision, and laparoscopic surgery combined with other techniques such as uterine nerve transection or uterine suspension. Some studies also compared different surgical tools, such as helium thermal coagulators versus electrodiathermy, or conservative laparoscopic surgery versus laparoscopic colorectal resection for deep infiltrating endometriosis. Laparoscopic Surgery vs. Diagnostic Laparoscopy Alone The evidence regarding the effect of laparoscopic surgery on overall pain relief compared to diagnostic laparoscopy alone was highly uncertain. At six months, one study reported a mean difference (MD) in pain scores of 0.90 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.31 to 1.49; very low-quality evidence), and at 12 months, the MD was 1.65 (95% CI 1.11 to 2.19; very low-quality evidence). A positive MD indicates pain relief, while a negative MD reflects worsening pain. No studies assessed live birth outcomes in this comparison. The impact of laparoscopic surgery on quality of life was also uncertain. For example, one study reported a EuroQol-5D index summary score at six months with an MD of 0.03 (95% CI -0.12 to 0.18; low-quality evidence). Similarly, the 12-item Short Form (SF-12) mental health component showed an MD of 2.30 (95% CI -4.50 to 9.10; low-quality evidence), and the physical health component had an MD of 2.70 (95% CI -2.90 to 8.30; low-quality evidence). However, laparoscopic surgery likely improves the rate of viable intrauterine pregnancies compared to diagnostic laparoscopy alone. The odds ratio (OR) for viable intrauterine pregnancy was 1.89 (95% CI 1.25 to 2.86; moderate-quality evidence) based on three RCTs involving 528 participants. The effect on ectopic pregnancy (MD 1.18, 95% CI 0.10 to 13.48; low-quality evidence) and miscarriage (MD 0.94, 95% CI 0.35 to 2.54; low-quality evidence) was uncertain. Adverse events were poorly reported, but no conversions to laparotomy were noted in either group (1 RCT, 341 participants). Laparoscopic Ablation and Uterine Nerve Transection vs. Diagnostic Laparoscopy The effect of laparoscopic ablation combined with uterine nerve transection on adverse events, such as vascular injury, was uncertain (OR 0.33, 95% CI 0.01 to 8.32; low-quality evidence). No studies evaluated outcomes such as overall pain, live birth, quality of life, viable intrauterine pregnancy, ectopic pregnancy, or miscarriage for this comparison. Laparoscopic Ablation vs. Laparoscopic Excision There was insufficient evidence to determine whether laparoscopic ablation or excision was superior in reducing overall pain at 12 months (MD 0.00, 95% CI -1.22 to 1.22; very low-quality evidence). No studies assessed outcomes such as pain at six months, live birth, quality of life, viable intrauterine pregnancy, ectopic pregnancy, miscarriage, or adverse events. Helium Thermal Coagulator vs. Electrodiathermy The comparison between helium thermal coagulators and electrodiathermy for laparoscopic treatment of endometriosis showed uncertain effects on quality of life. For example, the 30-item Endometriosis Health Profile (EHP-30) pain component at nine months had an MD of 6.68 (95% CI -3.07 to 16.43; very low-quality evidence). Other components, such as control and powerlessness (MD 4.79, 95% CI -6.92 to 16.50), emotional well-being (MD 6.17, 95% CI -3.95 to 16.29), and social support (MD 5.62, 95% CI -6.21 to 17.45), also showed very low-quality evidence. Adverse events were not estimable, and no studies evaluated outcomes such as pain, live birth, viable intrauterine pregnancy, ectopic pregnancy, or miscarriage. Authors' Conclusions The evidence is uncertain regarding whether laparoscopic surgery reduces overall pain associated with endometriosis compared to diagnostic laparoscopy alone. No data were available on live birth outcomes for any of the comparisons. However, moderate-quality evidence suggests that laparoscopic surgery increases the rate of viable intrauterine pregnancies confirmed by ultrasound compared to diagnostic laparoscopy alone. There was insufficient evidence to draw conclusions about the safety of laparoscopic surgery, particularly regarding adverse events. Further research is needed to explore the management of different subtypes of endometriosis and to compare laparoscopic interventions with lifestyle and medical treatments.
